title: Developing test plans and testing a solution

pages.c06-p01: Explain the following iterative approaches to testing: white box; black box; and system, unit and integration testing
pages.c06-p02: Create and use a test plan that identifies test procedures for use during and after development to check a system against success criteria
pages.c06-p03: Devise and use the following types of test data: valid, invalid and extreme

q.q: Which statement describes iterative testing?
o: Testing, fixing and retesting repeatedly during and after development
Testing every possible input value once the program is finished
Testing the program only once, at the very end of development
Testing carried out only by the end users of the system
q.why: Iterative means repeated cycles of test, fix and retest.

q.q: Why is testing carried out?
o: To translate the source code into machine code for the processor
To make the program run faster by removing unused code
To find errors before users do and check the program meets its requirements
To prove that the program contains no errors at all
q.why: Testing finds errors and checks requirements; it can never prove a program has no errors.

q.q: Which type of testing examines the internal logic of the code?
o: Black box testing
System testing
White box testing
Acceptance testing
q.why: White box testers can see and trace the code.

q.q: Which type of testing checks inputs against expected outputs without looking at the code?
o: White box testing
Black box testing
Unit testing
Dry run testing
q.why: Black box testing only considers inputs and outputs.

q.q: Who usually carries out black box testing?
o: The original programmer reading through the code
Independent testers or users who do not see the code
The compiler, as it translates the program
The programmer using breakpoints and trace tables
q.why: Black box testers use only inputs and outputs, which makes the testing more independent.

q.q: Who usually carries out white box testing?
o: The end user
The programmer
An independent tester who cannot see the code
The customer who ordered the system
q.why: White box testing needs knowledge of the code, so it is usually done by the programmer.

q.q: What is the aim of white box testing?
o: To check each function behaves as the requirements say, without seeing the code
To check that separately written modules work together
To check the finished system in a realistic setting
To execute every path, branch and condition in the code
q.why: White box testing aims to run every path; the second option is the aim of black box testing.

q.q: Which tools are typical of white box testing?
o: A test plan of inputs with expected outputs only
Dry runs, trace tables and breakpoints
Questionnaires and interviews with users
Syntax highlighting and auto-complete
q.why: White box testers trace through the code itself.

q.q: For the kayak hire program, a tester enters 4 hours and checks that the screen shows £40, as the price list says. Which approach is this?
o: White box testing
Unit testing
Integration testing
Black box testing
q.why: The tester checks an input against the expected output without looking at the code.

q.q: For the kayak hire program, a tester reads the ELSE IF chain and chooses hours so that every branch runs. Which approach is this?
o: Black box testing
White box testing
System testing
Null data testing
q.why: Choosing data from the code's structure is white box testing.

q.q: Good white box test data for a loop should make the body run how many times?
o: Exactly once, so the loop is not slowed down
As many times as possible, to test it fully
Zero times, once and more than once
Only the number of times the programmer expects
q.why: Testing zero, one and many repetitions checks the loop's boundaries.

q.q: Code finds the largest of three numbers a, b and c. Which set of white box tests is needed?
o: a largest only, as the code checks a first
a largest, b largest, c largest, and all three equal
Three random sets of numbers chosen by a user
c largest only, as that uses the ELSE branch
q.why: Every branch must run, and equal values test the edge case.

q.q: Which is an advantage of white box testing?
o: It is thorough: every line and path can be tested and hidden errors found
The tester need not be the programmer, so it is more independent
Tests can be planned as soon as the specification is written
It shows clearly where the user requirements are not met
q.why: Thoroughness is the white box advantage; the other three are black box advantages.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of white box testing?
o: Only some paths are tried, so errors may be missed
When a test fails the cause may not be clear
It may repeat tests the programmer has already done
It needs experienced programmers and is slow for large programs
q.why: White box testing is complex and slow; the other options are black box disadvantages.

q.q: Which is an advantage of black box testing?
o: Every line and path of the code can be tested
The tester knows exactly what data will test each path
Hidden errors deep in the code are found
The tester need not be the programmer, so the testing is more independent
q.why: Independence is a black box advantage; the others are white box advantages.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of black box testing?
o: It needs an experienced programmer who knows the code
When a test fails, the cause may not be clear
It is complex and slow for large programs
It can only be done after the system is released
q.why: The black box tester cannot see the code, so the cause of a failure may be unclear.

q.q: What is unit testing?
o: Testing one module, function or method on its own, as soon as it is written
Testing that separately written modules work correctly together
Testing the complete system against its specification
Testing the program with a single item of test data
q.why: Unit testing tests one part on its own, usually by its developer.

q.q: Why does unit testing count as white box testing?
o: The tester cannot see the code, only the inputs and outputs
It is carried out by end users in a realistic setting
The tester works from the code of that one small part
It uses the full test plan with realistic volumes of data
q.why: The developer tests their own code, so they can see its structure.

q.q: What is integration testing?
o: Testing one module on its own as soon as it has been written
Testing the complete, finished system against the requirements
Testing the program by reading the code line by line
Testing that separately written units work correctly together, especially the data passed between them
q.why: Integration testing checks the connections between modules.

q.q: What is system testing?
o: Testing the complete, finished system against its specification and requirements
Testing one function on its own using a trace table
Testing the data passed between two modules
Testing the computer hardware the system will run on
q.why: System testing treats the whole system as a black box using the full test plan.

q.q: What is the usual order of testing levels?
o: System, then integration, then unit
Unit, then integration, then system
Integration, then unit, then system
Unit, then system, then integration
q.why: Small parts first, then how they connect, then the whole.

q.q: A login function and a booking function each work on their own, but the booking function receives the wrong user ID from login. Which level of testing should find this?
o: Unit testing
Integration testing
White box testing of login only
Null data testing
q.why: The fault is in the data passed between two modules.

q.q: A library system's search function is tested by its programmer straight after it has been written. Which level of testing is this?
o: Integration testing
Unit testing
System testing
Black box testing
q.why: One module tested on its own by its developer is unit testing.

q.q: A finished cinema booking system is tested with realistic numbers of bookings against all of the client's requirements. Which level of testing is this?
o: Unit testing
Integration testing
White box testing
System testing
q.why: Testing the whole system against its requirements in a realistic setting is system testing.

q.q: How should system testing be carried out?
o: In a realistic setting with realistic volumes of data
By the programmer, using breakpoints in each method
On one module at a time as soon as it is written
Only with valid data, as invalid data was tested earlier
q.why: System testing uses the full test plan with valid, invalid and extreme data in realistic conditions.

q.q: An error is found during integration testing and fixed. What should happen next?
o: The program goes straight to the users, as it has now been fixed
Testing starts again from system testing, skipping unit tests
The earlier tests are repeated to check the fix has not broken anything
The test is removed from the test plan as it has passed
q.why: Fixing and repeating earlier tests is what makes the process iterative.

q.q: A pupil writes: "Integration testing tests that the whole system meets the requirements." What is wrong?
o: That describes unit testing; integration testing is done by end users
That describes system testing; integration testing is about the connections between modules
Nothing is wrong; integration and system testing are the same
That describes black box testing; integration testing is always white box
q.why: Integration is about connections; system testing is about the whole system.

q.q: Which answer best gives one difference between black box and white box testing?
o: White box looks at the code
Black box testing is better than white box testing
White box looks at the code, whereas black box only considers inputs and outputs
Black box only considers inputs and outputs, and so does white box
q.why: Make each difference a contrast between the two.

q.q: Why is black box testing suited to checking that user requirements are met?
o: It checks that each function behaves as the requirements say, from the user's point of view
It traces every line of code to find hidden errors
It is always carried out by the programmer who knows the code
It tests the data passed between modules
q.why: Black box testing checks behaviour against the requirements.

q.q: When can black box tests be planned?
o: Only after all the code has been written and compiled
Only after white box testing has been completed
Only during the evaluation of the finished system
As soon as the specification is written, before any code exists
q.why: Black box tests depend only on the requirements, so they can be planned early.

q.q: Why is it impossible for white box testing to guarantee a program is error-free?
o: White box testing only looks at the inputs and outputs
White box testing is only used on very small programs
The programmer cannot see the code during white box testing
It is impossible to test every possible case
q.why: Even thorough testing cannot try every possible input.

q.q: Which type of testing is a programmer using when stepping through a method with breakpoints to check each IF branch?
o: Black box testing
System testing
White box testing
Acceptance testing
q.why: Breakpoints and tracing through the code are white box tools.

q.q: What does each cycle of iterative testing do to the solution?
o: It makes it slower, as extra tests are added to the code
It removes features that failed their tests
It improves it, as faults found are fixed and the tests repeated
It replaces the test plan with a new one
q.why: Each test-fix-retest cycle improves the solution.

q.q: A program has three modules written by different programmers. Each passes its own tests. Why is integration testing still needed?
o: The modules may not work correctly together, for example when passing data
The modules have not been checked for syntax errors
Unit tests do not check the code's logic
Each module must be tested again by the same programmer
q.why: Passing unit tests does not prove the connections between modules work.

q.q: What is a test plan?
o: A diagram showing how a problem is broken down into modules
A table showing the value of each variable as a program runs
A table listing each test's number, purpose, test data, type, expected outcome, actual outcome and action
A list of every variable with its data type and validation
q.why: A test plan lists the tests to be carried out and links them to the success criteria.

q.q: When should a test plan be written?
o: Only if errors are found
During the evaluation only
After the program is released
Before testing is carried out
q.why: Planning first makes testing thorough and linked to the requirements.

q.q: What are success criteria?
o: The tests that have already passed during unit testing
The number of errors that were found during testing
The marks awarded by the moderator for a project
The user requirements that the finished system is checked against
q.why: Each test links back to a success criterion.

q.q: Which column is completed only when the test is actually run?
o: Expected outcome
Actual outcome
Purpose
Test data
q.why: The actual outcome records what really happened.

q.q: Which is the best expected outcome for entering 25 into an age field that accepts 11–18?
o: An error is shown to the user on the screen
The program works correctly with this data
Message "Age must be 11 to 18" is shown and the age is re-entered
The number 25 appears in the age box on screen
q.why: Expected outcomes must be specific; vague outcomes earn no marks.

q.q: In a test plan, what does the 'observed output' column record?
o: What actually happened when the test was run
What should happen when the test is run
The type of test data used in the test
Who carried out the test and when
q.why: Observed output is the textbook's name for the actual outcome.

q.q: What is recorded in the action column of a test plan?
o: The exact test data entered for each test
What should happen when the test is run
Which user requirement the test checks
Any correction made, and that the test was repeated
q.why: The action column records the fix and the retest.

q.q: Why does a test plan include a test number?
o: So each test can be referred to
So the tests run in the right order
So the computer can run the tests automatically
So the number of errors can be counted
q.why: Numbering lets each test be identified and referred to.

q.q: In the age test plan, test 2 entered 11 and showed an error message. The action was "Changed > 11 to >= 11; retested – accepted". What does this show?
o: A boundary error was found, fixed and the test repeated: evidence of iterative testing
The test data was wrong, so the test was removed from the plan
The program crashed and could not be fixed
The expected outcome was wrong, so it was changed to match the actual outcome
q.why: The fix and retest are evidence of iterative testing.

q.q: In the age test plan, test 4 entered "ten" and the program crashed. What action was taken?
o: An int.TryParse type check was added and the test repeated
A range check was changed from > to >=
The test was removed because text is not allowed
A presence check was added and the test repeated
q.why: The crash was fixed by adding a type check with int.TryParse.

q.q: What should happen after a test fails?
o: The program is corrected and the test is repeated
The expected outcome is changed to match what happened
The test is deleted from the test plan
The program is released, with the failure noted
q.why: Failed tests lead to a correction and a retest.

q.q: How are test plan results used later in a project?
o: They are used to write the program's source code
They replace the user requirements
They are used to choose the programming language
They feed into the evaluation of the solution
q.why: Test results provide evidence for the evaluation.

q.q: A test plan is used during development and after development. What is it used for after development?
o: Writing the code for each module
Deciding the data types of the variables
Testing the finished system
Drawing the flowcharts for each module
q.why: During development each part is tested as it is built; after, the finished system is tested.

q.q: Which is NOT normally a column in a test plan?
o: Type of test data used
Line number of the code being executed
Expected outcome of the test
Action taken after the test
q.why: Line numbers belong in a trace table, not a test plan.

q.q: In Unit 5, which parts of the test plan do moderators often find missing?
o: The test number and the purpose of each test
Extreme data and the action/retest column
The valid test data and the expected outcome
The title and the name of the programmer
q.why: Include tests on every boundary and record what you changed.

q.q: As well as the table of tests, what else does a full test plan document in industry record?
o: The features to be tested, the approach, the test environment, the staff involved and a schedule
The source code of the program and its comments
The user manual and installation instructions
The data dictionary and the wireframes
q.why: The test plan document also covers scope, approach, environment, staff and schedule.

q.q: In a test plan document, what is the test environment?
o: The room where the testers will sit
The list of tests that will not be carried out
The hardware and software the tests will be run on
The dates on which each test will be run
q.why: The test environment is the hardware and software used.

q.q: Your textbook's test plan has a column "Does observed match expected? (Y/N)". Why is this useful?
o: It records the type of test data used
It shows at a glance whether each test passed or failed
It tells the tester what data to enter
It shows which requirement each test checks
q.why: Comparing observed with expected shows pass or fail.

q.q: Why should each test in a test plan be linked to a success criterion?
o: So the tests can be run in alphabetical order
So testing checks that every user requirement has been met
So the programmer knows which line of code to test
So fewer tests are needed overall
q.why: Linking to the requirements makes testing thorough and purposeful.

q.q: Why is planning tests better than testing at random?
o: Random testing takes longer because each test is written down
Planned testing does not need any test data
Planned testing is thorough and covers every requirement and boundary
Random testing can only be used for black box testing
q.why: A test plan makes testing planned and thorough rather than random.

q.q: Which expected outcome would earn the mark in a test plan for a blank surname?
o: Message "Surname is required" is displayed and the user is asked again
An error happens when the surname is left blank
The program does not work properly with this data
Nothing is stored in the surname field of the file
q.why: Write precisely what should happen, including the message and re-input.

q.q: A test plan shows Expected outcome "Total £48" and Actual outcome "Total £60" for 6 hours of kayak hire. What should the tester do?
o: Change the expected outcome to £60 so the test passes
Ignore the result, as the program did not crash
Delete the test, as 6 hours is outside the normal range
Record the failure, correct the program and repeat the test
q.why: A mismatch is a failed test; fix the program and retest.

q.q: A test plan row reads: Purpose "Accept lowest age", Test data 11, Type Extreme. Which is the best expected outcome?
o: Age 11 is accepted and the program moves on
Age 11 is rejected with an error message
The program asks for the age again
The program shows "Age must be 11–18"
q.why: 11 is on the limit, so it is extreme data and should be accepted.

q.q: A test plan row has Test data "ten" for an age field. Which type of test data should be recorded?
o: Valid
Extreme
Null
Invalid
q.why: Text in a number field is the wrong type, so it is invalid data.

q.q: A test plan row has Test data (nothing) for an age field. Which type of test data should be recorded?
o: Invalid
Extreme
Valid
Null
q.why: A blank entry is null data.

q.q: Which column of a test plan states which requirement a test is checking?
o: Test data
Actual outcome
Purpose / description
Action
q.why: The purpose explains what is being tested and which requirement it checks.

q.q: A tester fills in the expected outcome after running the test, copying what the program did. Why is this poor practice?
o: The expected outcome must come from the requirements, or a wrong result would look like a pass
The expected outcome must be left blank until the evaluation is written
The expected outcome must always be the word "Error"
The expected outcome is filled in by the user, not the tester
q.why: Expected outcomes are planned before testing so actual results can be compared with them.

q.q: In a test plan document, what is the test strategy?
o: The dates on which each test will be carried out
The tests themselves: what will be tested and how
The names of the staff who will run the tests
The hardware the tests will run on
q.why: The test strategy is the set of tests; the schedule, staff and environment are recorded separately.

q.q: Why might a test plan document state features that will NOT be tested?
o: Because those features have too many errors to fix
So the user does not find out about them
To make clear what is outside the scope of testing, and why
Because only black box testing records features
q.why: The document records which features will and will not be tested, with reasons.

q.q: A programmer's test plan contains only valid data tests, all of which passed. Why is this not enough?
o: Valid data tests never pass on the first attempt
A test plan must always contain exactly five tests
Valid data can only be tested by the end users
It does not show how the program handles boundaries, invalid or blank input
q.why: A thorough plan includes extreme, invalid and null data too.

q.q: What is valid (normal) test data?
o: Data on the limits of the accepted range, which should be accepted
Data that breaks the rules, which should be rejected
Typical data inside the accepted range, which should be accepted
Data left blank, which should be rejected
q.why: Valid data is typical and accepted.

q.q: What is extreme (boundary) test data?
o: Data just outside the limits, which should be rejected
Valid data on the limits of the accepted range, which should be accepted
Very large values that should always be rejected
Data of the wrong type, which should be rejected
q.why: Extreme data is valid: on the edge of the range, not outside it.

q.q: What is invalid (erroneous) test data?
o: Data that breaks the rules, out of range or the wrong type, which should be rejected
Data on the limits of the range, which should be accepted
Typical data inside the range, which should be accepted
Data that has been entered twice to check it
q.why: Invalid data should be rejected with an error message.

q.q: What is null test data?
o: Nothing entered at all
The value 0
A very large number
A negative number
q.why: Null means the input is left blank.

q.q: A form accepts a quantity from 1 to 50. Which value is extreme data?
q.why: 50 is on the upper limit and should be accepted. 51 is invalid.

q.q: A program accepts ages from 11 to 18. Which is invalid data?
q.why: 19 is outside the range.

q.q: A program accepts ages from 11 to 18. Which is valid (normal) data?
q.why: 15 is typical data inside the range. 11 and 18 are extreme.

q.q: Which statement about extreme data is true?
o: It is valid data on the limits of the accepted range
It is always a very large or very small number
It is the same as null data, left blank
It is out of range, so it should be rejected
q.why: Extreme data is on the boundary and should be accepted.

q.q: A test mark must be from 0 to 100. A pupil gives 101 as extreme data. Why is this wrong?
o: 101 is valid data, as it is close to the limit
101 is null data, as it cannot be stored
101 is extreme data; the pupil is correct
101 is outside the range, so it is invalid; extreme data is 0 or 100
q.why: This is the most common mistake: extreme data is valid and sits on the limit.

q.q: For a mark out of 0 to 100, which set gives one valid, one extreme and one invalid value, in that order?
q.why: 57 is typical, 100 is on the limit, 101 is outside the range.

q.q: Why are values just outside the limits, such as −1 and 101 for a 0–100 range, especially useful test data?
o: They are the values users enter most often
They test whether the program can store very large numbers
They check that blank entries are rejected
They catch boundary mistakes such as < written instead of <=
q.why: Values just beyond the boundary reveal off-by-one comparison errors.

q.q: A password must be 8 to 20 characters. Which is extreme test data?
o: A password of 12 characters
A password of 21 characters
A password of exactly 20 characters
A blank password
q.why: Exactly 8 or exactly 20 characters sit on the limits.

q.q: A password must be 8 to 20 characters. Which is invalid test data?
o: A password of 7 characters
A password of 8 characters
A password of 12 characters
A password of 20 characters
q.why: 7 characters is outside the allowed length.

q.q: A password must be 8 to 20 characters. What is the expected result for a blank password?
o: Accepted, as it is extreme data
Accepted, as blank passwords are shorter than 20
Rejected with an error message, as it is null data
The program should crash
q.why: Null data should be rejected with an error message.

q.q: A gym accepts members aged 16 to 70. Which is the best way to state a piece of test data?
o: 16 – extreme
16 – extreme, because it is the lowest age the gym accepts
16 – this should work
16 – valid, because it is a number
q.why: State the type and say why, using the rules in the scenario.

q.q: For an age field accepting 11 to 18, which value is the best invalid test of the wrong type?
o: "fifteen"
(blank)
q.why: "fifteen" is the wrong data type. 19 and 10 are out of range; blank is null.

q.q: A program accepts 1 to 14 nights. Which list contains both extreme values?
o: 0 and 15
1 and 14
2 and 13
1 and 15
q.why: Extreme values are on the limits themselves.

q.q: A program accepts 1 to 14 nights. Which values are just outside the limits?
o: 1 and 14
7 and 8
0 and 15
q.why: 0 and 15 are invalid boundary values that catch < versus <= mistakes.

q.q: What is the expected result for extreme test data?
o: Accepted
Rejected with an error message
The program asks for the data again
The program crashes
q.why: Extreme data is valid, so it should be accepted.

q.q: Where should test data come from?
o: Values chosen at random by the tester
The largest and smallest numbers the computer can store
The values used in the program's comments
The rules given in the scenario, such as the stated range or length
q.why: Test data must come from the rules in the scenario.

q.q: A test of the value 0 for a 0–100 mark is rejected by the program. What does this suggest?
o: The program is working correctly, as 0 is invalid
The range check probably uses > 0 instead of >= 0
The program needs a presence check for the mark
The test data is null, so it should be rejected
q.why: 0 is extreme data and should be accepted; rejection points to a boundary error.

q.q: Which phrase is another name for invalid data in some textbooks?
o: Normal data
Boundary data
Erroneous data
Null data
q.why: Invalid data is also called erroneous data. Normal is valid; boundary is extreme.

q.q: Which phrase is another name for extreme data?
o: Erroneous data
Boundary data
Normal data
Null data
q.why: Extreme data is valid data on the boundary of the range.

q.q: A field accepts a surname of 2 to 30 letters. Which test value is extreme data?
o: A surname of exactly 2 letters
A surname of 15 letters
A surname of just 1 letter
A blank surname field
q.why: Exactly 2 letters is on the lower limit and should be accepted.

q.q: A theatre allows bookings of 1 to 8 tickets. Which set of test data is most complete?
o: 4, 1, 8, 0, 9, "two" and blank
4, 5 and 6
1 and 8 only
q.why: It covers valid, both extremes, values just outside each limit, wrong type and null.

q.q: A theatre allows bookings of 1 to 8 tickets. What is the expected result for 9 tickets?
o: Accepted, as it is extreme data
Accepted, as it is valid data
Rejected with an error message
Treated as null data
q.why: 9 is just outside the limit, so it is invalid and should be rejected.

q.q: A theatre allows bookings of 1 to 8 tickets. What type of data is 1?
o: Invalid
Null
Erroneous
Extreme
q.why: 1 is on the lower limit, so it is extreme (valid) data.

q.q: A program checks a score with if (score > 0 && score <= 100). The rules say 0 to 100 is valid. Which test would reveal the error?
o: Entering 50, which should be accepted and is accepted
Entering 0, which should be accepted but is rejected
Entering 100, which should be accepted and is accepted
Entering 101, which should be rejected and is rejected
q.why: Extreme data at the lower limit exposes > written instead of >=.

q.q: The rules say a score from 0 to 100 is valid, but the code tests if (score >= 0 && score < 100). Which test value exposes this?
o: Entering 0
Entering 50
Entering 100
Entering −1
q.why: 100 should be accepted, but < 100 rejects it.

q.q: A temperature sensor program accepts readings from −20 to 50. Which value is extreme data?
q.why: −20 is on the lower limit, so it is extreme and accepted.

q.q: A temperature sensor program accepts readings from −20 to 50. Which value is invalid data?
q.why: −21 is just outside the lower limit.

q.q: Extreme data is described as data on the limits of the range. What else can it include?
o: Values of the wrong data type, such as text
Blank entries where nothing is typed
Values that the system should reject
Very large or very small values the system must cope with
q.why: Extreme data can also mean very large or very small values the system must handle.

q.q: A product code must be exactly 6 characters. Which values give extreme and invalid tests?
o: Extreme: 5 or 7 characters; invalid: 6 characters
Extreme: 6 characters; invalid: 5 or 7 characters
Extreme: 1 character; invalid: 100 characters
Extreme: blank; invalid: 6 characters
q.why: With an exact length, the limit itself is 6; one either side is invalid.

q.q: A pupil gives "−5" as null data for an age field. Why is this wrong?
o: −5 is extreme data, as it is a negative number
−5 is valid data, as it is a whole number
Null data means nothing entered; −5 is invalid data
Null data must always be the value 0
q.why: Null data is a blank entry, not a negative or zero value.

q.q: Why is the value 0 not the same as null data?
o: 0 is always valid data, but null is always extreme data
0 is a value that has been entered; null means nothing was entered
0 is text, but null is a number
0 and null are the same, as both mean no value
q.why: Null means the input was left blank.

q.q: For a 0 to 100 mark, a tester uses 57, 0, 100, −1, 101, "sixty" and blank. How many of these should be accepted?
q.why: 57 (valid), 0 and 100 (extreme) are accepted; the rest should be rejected.
